question: Jews and Muslims both confess one God and refuse to worship Jesus. Isn't Christianity the faith that strayed from the God of Abraham?

ledger.heading: Twentieth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the morality area, and the area "Other religions, and those who never heard"

shortAnswer: Christianity, Judaism and Islam share more than most of their members know: one God, the Creator, who called Abraham, spoke through Moses and the prophets, gives his commands and will judge the world. They part at one point above all, and it is Jesus. Judaism holds that he was not the Messiah, since the age of peace the Messiah was to bring has not come, and that to worship him breaks the oneness of God. Islam honors him as the Messiah and a prophet, born of Mary, and holds that God took him up to himself, but denies that he is God's Son or that he was crucified. Christians confess that he was crucified, rose, and is the eternal Son within the one God. That is a real difference, not a misunderstanding, and both neighbors deserve to have it stated honestly. Whether Christianity strayed turns on whether what it says about Jesus is true.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
The objection comes from the two faiths that stand nearest to Christianity, and it comes from reverence, not contempt. The Jewish scholar Solomon Schechter, in his *Studies in Judaism* (1896), gathered the teaching of the rabbis on God into a single statement: "The unity of God is the keystone of dogmatic Judaism." God tells the prophets, Schechter's summary goes on, "'I am the first,' ... which implies that he had no father, and the words, 'There is no God besides me,' mean that he has no son." Israel Abrahams, a Jewish scholar who taught rabbinic literature at Cambridge, wrote in his short book *Judaism* that what kept Jews from accepting much of the teaching of Jesus was above all "the deep-seated conviction that the Pauline Christianity was a denial of the Jewish monotheism."

The Qur'an says the same from another side. In Mohammed Marmaduke Pickthall's translation, it confesses of God that "He begetteth not nor was begotten" (Qur'an 112:3), says that the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, "was only a messenger of Allah, and His word which He conveyed unto Mary, and a spirit from Him" (4:171), and says of the cross that "they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them" (4:157), adding, "But Allah took him up unto Himself" (4:158). Jews and Muslims read these texts within their own long traditions of interpretation, and neither faith speaks with one voice on every point, but on these the common confession of each is plain.

At full strength the objection says this. Abraham turned from the gods of his fathers to the one God. Moses gave Israel the confession, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4, BSB). The prophets thundered against every rival to God's glory. Judaism kept that faith through exile and persecution, and Islam, by its own account, calls people back to it: "follow the religion of Abraham, the upright" (Qur'an 3:95). Christianity alone took a man, a Jewish teacher executed by Rome, and worshipped him. Whatever its virtues, it is the one of the three that left the God of Abraham.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
Much of it. The three faiths share the one God and much of the same story, and a Christian who speaks of either neighbor as if it worshipped an idol hasn't understood it.

Judaism, as its own scholars describe it, confesses one God, eternal and without body, whose unity is the keystone of the faith; it lives by the Torah, the written law of Moses with the oral tradition the rabbis set down in the Mishnah about the year 200 and expounded in the Talmud; and it hopes for the Messiah, though Jews, Abrahams notes, have differed on whether that hope is for a personal Messiah. The great medieval teacher Moses Maimonides set out thirteen principles, which Abrahams lists: among them the existence, unity, incorporeality and eternity of God, that worship is offered to God alone, prophecy, the Law revealed from heaven and never abrogated, reward and punishment, the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection of the dead. Abrahams adds that no council of rabbis ever made them binding, though they stand in the traditional prayer books. The Messianic hope, in the words of the scholar J. H. Greenstone, whom Abrahams quotes, is of "universal peace, an age of justice and of righteousness, an age in which all men will recognise that God is One and His name One." And Judaism has never been the religion of earning favor that Christians have sometimes made it. Among the rabbis' sayings Schechter gathered is that "the world is judged by grace, yet all according to the works wrought." Nor is rabbinic Judaism a stage on the way to Christianity, or a museum of the faith Jesus knew. It is a living faith, with its own unbroken life of prayer, study and law, and its teachers have their own reasons for reading Israel's Scriptures as they do.

Islam, as Muslims confess it, holds to *tawhid*, the oneness and uniqueness of God, which is central to the faith. It receives the Qur'an as God's word revealed to Muhammad, whom it calls "the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (Qur'an 33:40), and it honors the prophets before him, Abraham, Moses and Jesus among them. Muslims keep what are called the five pillars: the confession of faith, the daily prayers, almsgiving, the fast of Ramadan and the pilgrimage to Mecca. The Qur'an tells Muslims to say to Jews and Christians, "our Allah and your Allah is One" (29:46), and it gives Jesus high honor, as "a word from him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary" (3:45).

It is true, too, that Christians have done grave wrong to both. For more than a thousand years many Christians read Matthew 27:25 as a curse on every later generation of Jews, and, as the Study Bible's note on Matthew 27 records, that reading was preached in Holy Week, staged in passion plays and "used to justify contempt, expulsions, and mob violence against Jewish communities." Crusaders massacred the Jews of Worms and Mainz in 1096, and in 1543 Martin Luther wrote *On the Jews and Their Lies*, as the note on John 16 records. Crusaders killed the Muslims of Jerusalem in 1099. That reading of Scripture is false, and this site rejects it, as its notes on Romans 11 say. The Second Vatican Council's *Nostra Aetate* (1965) taught that what happened in the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today; after the Shoah the Vatican's *We Remember* (1998) and many Protestant bodies spoke in the same direction, among them the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, which in 1994 repudiated Luther's anti-Jewish writings, as the note on Matthew 27 records.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
The first followers of Jesus were not pagans who forgot the Shema. They were Jews who prayed it. Jesus himself, asked which commandment is first, answered with it: "Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One" (Mark 12:29, BSB). Peter preached that "The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13, BSB). Paul, a Pharisee "extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers" (Galatians 1:14, BSB), wrote, "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist" (1 Corinthians 8:6, BSB). That sentence is the Shema read again: the one God and the one Lord, with Jesus inside the confession, not beside it as a second god.

How early that happened is a matter of history, and the Study Bible's note on John 1 sets out the case. Richard Bauckham and Larry Hurtado argue that the earliest Christians, all of them Jewish monotheists, included Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God from the start, giving him the role of creator that Jewish monotheism reserved for God alone; and the Jewish scholar Daniel Boyarin, as the note reports, argues that ideas of a divine Word alongside God were at home in first-century Judaism before the rabbis ruled them out. If they are right, the worship of Jesus was not a later Gentile corruption of a Jewish teacher's message. It began among Jews who believed they had not left the God of Abraham but seen him act.

The second evidence is the claim on which everything rests: that Jesus was crucified and raised. Here the three faiths divide sharply. Christians say it happened. Muslims, following the Qur'an, say it did not happen as it appeared. Jewish readers, as the Study Bible's note on Mark 16 records, have generally held that whatever the disciples experienced, it didn't make Jesus the Messiah, since the Messianic age of peace did not come. The crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is attested by Christian and Roman sources alike, and this library's pages on the historical Jesus set out the evidence for it and for the empty tomb. The resurrection is the claim a historian can argue for and no historian can compel.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is an argument about where the three faiths truly differ, and about what the charge of straying depends on.
steps: Judaism, Christianity and Islam confess one God, the Creator, who called Abraham, spoke through Moses and the prophets, and will judge the world.

They differ above all about Jesus: Judaism holds that he wasn't the Messiah and that worshipping him breaks God's unity; Islam honors him as Messiah and prophet but denies that he is God's Son and that he was crucified; Christianity confesses him crucified, risen and the eternal Son within the one God.

The Christian confession arose among Jewish monotheists who confessed the Shema and included Jesus within it, and it rests on a claim about events, the crucifixion and the resurrection, that can be weighed.
sections.conclusion: So: Christianity did not, by its own account, leave the God of Abraham; it claims that the God of Abraham has acted in Jesus, and whether it strayed turns on whether that claim is true.
sections.after: The three faiths can state that difference plainly, as a difference, without contempt. The weight sits on the third step. Both neighbors deny that worshipping Jesus can be squared with the oneness of God, however early it began. That denial is weighed next.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply is that age and sincerity don't make a belief consistent. If God has no son, as Schechter's rabbis read "There is no God besides me," and if God "begetteth not," as the Qur'an says, then the earliest Christians were wrong from the start, and calling the Son "one Lord" within the Shema only renames the problem. A Jewish reader will add, as the Study Bible's note on Mark 8 records, that the Messiah was to defeat Israel's enemies, rebuild the temple and gather the exiles, and Jesus did none of these, and that the law calls anyone hung on a tree "under God's curse" (Deuteronomy 21:23, BSB).

These replies are serious, and they should be heard as what they are: the convictions of faithful people about the God Christians also worship. Christians answer the first by saying what they don't mean. They don't mean that God has a son as creatures do, or a second god beside him, or that Mary is divine; the Nicene Creed confesses the Son "begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father," and it confesses one God. Whether that confession keeps God's unity is exactly the point in dispute, and an argument can show why Christians hold it without making a Jew or a Muslim accept it. To the second, Christians answer that the Messiah came first to suffer, as Jesus taught that "the Son of Man must suffer many things ... and that He must be killed and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31, BSB), and that he will come again to finish what he began. Jewish readers answer that this changes the hope rather than fulfilling it. Neither side should pretend the other has no reply.

What can be said is narrower. The charge that Christianity strayed is a charge that its claim about Jesus is false. If he was not raised, the charge stands, and Paul said so himself (1 Corinthians 15:17). If he was, then the God of Abraham has done something new, and the Christian confession is not a departure from him but an account of what he did.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: Whether Christians and Muslims worship the same God is a question Christians answer differently, as the site's Honest Answer on Christianity and Islam sets out, much turning on the difference between referring to God and describing him rightly. How the church should relate to the Jewish people today is answered in several ways, and the Study Bible's notes on Romans 11 set them out in their holders' terms without choosing: that the church has replaced Israel, a view much of the church held for centuries, often in harsh forms, and many churches now reject; a milder view of fulfilment in Christ; covenant theology's one people of God with Jewish and Gentile branches; dispensational readings that keep a distinct future for the Jewish people; and two-covenant readings, held by some and not by most churches. What Paul meant by "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26) is read in more than one way. And whether the resurrection happened is left to the pages that argue it.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Christians differ on the questions just named and on how to speak of other faiths: some stress what Christians share with Jews and Muslims, others the distance between them. What all confess is the faith of the creeds, one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ crucified and risen; and on every view, as the Study Bible's note on Romans 11 says, contempt for Jews has no ground in Scripture. Paul told Gentile believers, "do not boast over those branches. ... You do not support the root, but the root supports you" (Romans 11:18, BSB), and said of Israel that "God's gifts and His call are irrevocable" (Romans 11:29, BSB). Nothing on this page is a claim about any modern state.
